description: Team Vyuha Cosmic from JNNCE is dedicated to exploring the outer horizons of our solar system for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Drawing inspiration from the strategic precision of an ancient Indian Vyuha, we utilize data science and orbital mechanics to analyze deep-space anomalies. Our objective is to build tools that map raw cosmic coordinates into structured insights, advancing open-source exploration.
summary:
Optical satellites are often blinded by dense storm clouds, wildfire smoke, and darkness during critical disasters. To solve this, Team Vyuha Cosmic developed Dancing with the SARs, an interactive, all-weather web dashboard that turns raw Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data into rapid disaster intelligence.
Using geocoded NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band (L2 GCOV) and Sentinel-1 C-band granules from NASA’s ASF Vertex portal, our Python pipeline converts backscatter intensities into decibels (dB), performs temporal differencing (After - Before), and generates de-speckled RGBA change overlays alongside standardized scientific reports. Built with Leaflet.js, our live web app features an interactive Before/After Swipe Slider, radar/optical opacity controls, and live NASA EONET integration across five global disaster zones—including monsoon flooding in Shivamogga (India), Kilauea volcanic activity, Amazon deforestation, California wildfires, and a Red Sea oil spill.
details:
What It Does & Key Benefits
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive, all-weather Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) visualization dashboard that detects and quantifies Earth surface changes through dense cloud cover, volcanic ash, wildfire smoke, and darkness. Unlike raw satellite archives that require specialized GIS software to interpret, our platform lets emergency responders, researchers, and citizens compare pre-event and post-event radar states side by side using an interactive Before / After Swipe Slider, radar/optical opacity controls, and automated scientific reports.

How We Built It (Pipeline & Tech Stack)

  1. SAR Data Acquisition & Preprocessing (Python, Kaggle, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow): We queried NASA’s ASF Vertex portal using Earthdata credentials to retrieve geocoded NASA-ISRO NISAR (L2 GCOV) and Sentinel-1 C-band granules on matching orbital tracks. Our Python pipeline converts linear backscatter intensities (HHHH/HVHV and VV/VH) into logarithmic decibels (10 * log10), computes temporal differencing (After - Before), applies morphological de-speckling filters to remove radar salt-and-pepper noise, and exports transparent RGBA overlays alongside standardized report.json metrics.
  2. Interactive Mission Control Web App (HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js): We built a lightweight, zero-backend web interface hosted on GitHub Pages that renders high-resolution Esri World Imagery tiles, custom pointer-driven swipe comparisons, and live NASA EONET real-time natural event tracking across any desktop or mobile browser.

Intended Impact & Design Considerations
We prioritized multi-band versatility (combining L-band vegetation/soil penetration with C-band surface roughness sensitivity) and local-to-global relevance. Alongside global events—Kilauea volcanic activity (Hawaii), Amazon deforestation (Brazil), California wildfires (USA), and a Red Sea oil spill (Yemen)—we analyzed monsoon waterlogging right in our home region of Shivamogga & Bhadra Reservoir, Karnataka, India, demonstrating how open orbital radar supports local flood resilience
